CASE 01 · Email threat response

Strengthening Cyber Resilience through Phishing Email Investigation and Response in Healthcare Organizations

+
MXToolbox VirusTotal Splunk SpamAssassin PhishTool

Context

MediSure Health Network relies heavily on digital technology, which also makes it a target. One morning, staff received an email styled as a vendor invoice. It was a phishing attempt built to steal patient information and financial records. The systems were secure, but employees were the exposed point.

Purpose

Reduce immediate risk, improve future readiness, and stay compliant with HIPAA, while protecting MediSure’s reputation, operations and finances.

Investigation phases

  1. Review the suspicious emails.
  2. Validate domains and sender details.
  3. Analyse attachments and links for hidden threats.
  4. Examine network traffic with SIEM tools.
  5. Respond: block domains, reset accounts, isolate affected endpoints, update email filters.
  6. Monitor continuously for similar threats.
  7. Report and document everything.

Key objectives

  • Identify phishing indicators in headers, sender data and embedded links.
  • Validate sender authenticity with SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks.
  • Detect payloads and credential harvesting in links and attachments.
  • Correlate inbound and outbound traffic against known malicious IPs and domains.
  • Contain the threat and train staff to recognise similar attacks.

Outcome

Phishing attempts were identified and contained, the likelihood of future attacks dropped, staff awareness rose, and compliance improved. Employees became the first line of defence.

CASE 02 · SIEM and detection engineering

SIEM Implementation & SOC Detection Engineering on Thornbury Wealth Partners

+
Splunk SPL Windows EventCodes Threat intel lookups
3 offices: London, New York, Toronto
2 compromised accounts
142 MB client data exfiltrated
7 detection rules built

Objective

Detect and investigate a coordinated cyber attack against a UK-based financial services firm across three offices, using Splunk.

What I found

  • Brute force attacks that led to two compromised accounts.
  • Unauthorised privilege escalation.
  • 142 MB of client data sent to an external C2 server.
  • Backdoor accounts created for persistent access.
  • Ransomware deployed across multiple file servers.

What I built

SPL queries correlating failed logins, Windows EventCodes, outbound traffic anomalies and threat intelligence lookups. The result was 7 detection rules, scheduled alerts with severity classifications, and a SOC dashboard that brings every finding into one operational view.

CASE 03 · Vulnerability management

Vulnerability Assessment & Network Scan on CyberTech Solutions

+
Nessus Ansible Python / Shell Ubuntu Kali Linux Gmail SMTP

Context

CyberTech Solutions needed to find and fix vulnerabilities in its Linux systems and web applications. Manual assessment was slow, and unaddressed weaknesses risked a breach and lost client trust.

What I did

  • Ran credentialed Nessus scans on Linux servers and web applications.
  • Automated email reporting through Gmail SMTP to speed up tracking and response.
  • Automated patching with Ansible, driven by Python and shell scripts.
  • Produced detailed stakeholder reports covering vulnerabilities, remediation steps and patch status.

Outcome

Less exposure through timely fixes, less manual work and fewer errors through automation, and a stronger security offering for CyberTech.

CASE 04 · Malware analysis (simulated critical-infrastructure incident)

Malware Threat Intelligence & SOC Response for Grid Sentinel OT Security

+
FLARE VM ProcMon RegShot Wireshark FakeNet-NG MITRE ATT &CK Evidence-led lab

Investigation scope

Independent FLARE-VM malware analysis lab, 9–10 November 2026. A hash-named Windows executable was examined through static inspection and controlled execution. “Grid Sentinel OT Security” is the simulated critical-infrastructure scenario, not a claim of a live customer incident. Objective: determine what the sample actually did, preserve evidence, and distinguish confirmed observations from suspected behaviour.

01 / Establish the baseline and inspect the executable

  • Recorded the sample identifier (SHA-256): c8f5d3f153fab81b07f3e666e13bcbd01d696a7efa4ae0c8dc81c054443e5b67. The hash is taken from the supplied walkthrough / filename.
  • Inspected PE dependencies in Dependency Walker: MSCOREE.DLL, KERNEL32.DLL, KERNELBASE.DLL and NTDLL.DLL. The _CorExeMain entry suggests a managed .NET executable; it does not identify a malware family.
  • Reviewed the executable manifest in Resource Hacker: requestedExecutionLevel = asInvoker. Ran Sysinternals Strings, but did not independently validate meaningful extracted strings from the available screenshot.
  • Prepared a Windows 10 FLARE-VM in VirtualBox. Adapter 1 was host-only; the captured guest address was 192.168.102.101/24 with no visible default gateway. Host-only networking does not guarantee separation from the host.

02 / Observe network behaviour — FakeNet-NG + Wireshark

  • Started FakeNet-NG to simulate DNS and HTTP responses and captured traffic with Wireshark. Distinguished Windows background certificate-check traffic to ctldl.windowsupdate.com from sample-related activity.
  • After execution, FakeNet-NG logged a DNS query for fortyfive5.ydns.eu attributed to the hash-named executable, followed by an attempted TCP connection to 192.0.2.123:5212.
  • Wireshark showed repeated DNS queries for the same domain and TCP SYN attempts. 192.0.2.123 is a simulated address in this environment, not proof of an external attacker server.
  • Assessment: attempted outbound communication and possible C2-related behaviour. The captures do not independently demonstrate successful external C2, regular beacon intervals or data exfiltration.

03 / Trace process execution — ProcMon

  • Opened Process Monitor → Process Tree to correlate the sample with related child processes and their lifetimes.
  • Observed multiple instances of the hash-named executable and associated processes including ermages.exe, cmd.exe and WerFault.exe. Process creation is an observation; malicious purpose requires additional corroboration.
  • Noted that the sample presented “License Review Application” metadata. This could warrant masquerading checks, but deception was not proven.
  • Next validation would compare full image paths, command lines, signatures, hashes and precise process-create events to determine which children were actually launched by the sample.

04 / Compare registry state — RegShot

  • Captured and compared registry snapshots before and after the analysis window. RegShot reported 92 keys added and 21 deleted.
  • Reviewed registry deltas, including Windows AppModel and cache entries. The raw counts alone cannot attribute changes to the malware.
  • A Run-key persistence mechanism was described in the training walkthrough, but was not verified in the available RegShot evidence. Therefore persistence is not reported as confirmed.

Findings and confidence

Finding Evidence-based assessment
DNS query to fortyfive5.ydns.eu Observed in FakeNet-NG and Wireshark
Outbound TCP attempts Observed to simulated 192.0.2.123:5212
Additional processes Observed in ProcMon Process Tree
Registry changes 92 added / 21 deleted; malware attribution unconfirmed
Registry persistence / external C2 / exfiltration Not independently confirmed

Indicators to investigate

  • Domain: fortyfive5.ydns.eu — observed DNS request; candidate IOC requiring external reputation checks.
  • SHA-256: c8f5d3f153fab81b07f3e666e13bcbd01d696a7efa4ae0c8dc81c054443e5b67 — sample identifier.
  • Process: ermages.exe — observed in process tree; verify file path and hash.
  • 192.0.2.123 — FakeNet-simulated endpoint; exclude from external threat-intelligence blocking lists.

SOC decision and response

Escalate for suspicious sample execution and attempted outbound communication. Preserve sanitized process-tree, DNS/TCP, and registry-diff evidence; correlate process IDs with packet timestamps; validate the domain and file hash against reputable threat-intelligence sources. Keep the lab isolated, power down and restore a known-clean pre-execution snapshot. No real endpoint containment, YARA deployment, production blocking or stakeholder briefing is claimed as completed.

MITRE ATT &CK — hypotheses, not confirmed detections

T1071.001 (Web Protocols): potential C2 communication, but sample-originated HTTP C2 was not proven. T1547.001 (Registry Run Keys): persistence was expected in the walkthrough, not confirmed in the registry comparison. T1036 (Masquerading): a possible interpretation of the application metadata, not established intent.

Investigation evidence — actual lab screenshots

Investigation evidence gallery

Six original lab screenshots, organised by investigation stage. Select any image for a closer view.

Case study conclusion

This lab demonstrates a repeatable SOC workflow: establish a baseline, inspect static indicators, execute under controlled monitoring, correlate host and network evidence, assess confidence, and recommend defensible next actions. The key lesson was to avoid mistaking suspicious indicators or training-guide expectations for confirmed compromise.

CASE 05 · Threat intelligence

Strengthening Cyber Threat Intelligence and Malware Detection on NorthByte Cybersecurity

+
VirusTotal Python YARA MITRE ATT &CK Kali Linux

Objective

Take one suspicious file hash through the full threat intelligence lifecycle, from "is this file malicious?" to a report a stakeholder can act on.

What I did

  • Triaged the hash and reached a malware verdict with VirusTotal, using Python automation scripts.
  • Researched the sample and investigated the associated threat intelligence.
  • Wrote and tested a custom YARA detection rule.
  • Mapped the attack lifecycle to the MITRE ATT &CK framework.
  • Delivered a formal threat intelligence report covering IOCs, threat analysis, and detection and prevention recommendations. The stakeholder is not named for confidentiality reasons.

Takeaway

A single hash can unlock an entire threat picture if you know how to pull the thread. The work showed me why threat intelligence matters beyond alert triage: wider context, attack techniques and detection opportunities.
